message.content:
The last common ancestor of a lion (Panthera leo) and a zebra (Equus quagga) is the **last common ancestor of all placental mammals (Eutheria)**.  
This ancestor lived roughly **100 million years ago** during the early Cretaceous period, before the diversification of the major mammalian orders such as Carnivora (to which lions belong) and Perissodactyla (to which zebras belong).
message.reasoning: The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) are both mammals, but they belong to different orders: lions are Carnivora, zebras are Perissodactyla. Their common ancestor would be at the level of the last common ancestor of all placental mammals, or maybe earlier. But we can give a more precise answer: The last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the last common ancestor of all placental mammals (Eutheria). That ancestor lived around 100 million years ago. So the answer: The last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of all placental mammals, which existed about 100 million years ago. Alternatively, we could mention that the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the last common ancestor of all eutherian mammals. So the answer: The last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of all placental mammals, which lived around 100 million years ago. We can also mention that the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the clade that includes the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla. So the answer: The last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of all placental mammals, which lived around 100 million years ago.
